title: Graphs of Logarithmic Functions
learningObjective: Graph logarithmic functions and determine the domain, range, and asymptotes.

faqs.question: What does the basic graph of a logarithmic function look like?
faqs.answer:
The parent logarithmic graph rises slowly, sweeping steeply upward near a vertical boundary on the left and then leveling off into a gentle, ever-increasing climb as it moves right. It never turns around, but it also never rises as dramatically as an exponential function does — logarithmic growth is famously slow.

\( g(x) = \log_2(x) \) climbs forever, but ever more slowly, hugging a vertical boundary on the left.

faqs.question: What is a vertical asymptote, and why does \( g(x) = \log_b(x) \) have one at x = 0?
faqs.answer: A vertical asymptote is a vertical line that a graph gets closer and closer to (without touching) as the input approaches some specific x-value. For \( g(x) = \log_b(x) \), that boundary is x = 0, because the logarithm's domain requires a positive argument (faq-4 in EL3) — as x shrinks toward 0 from the positive side, \( \log_b(x) \) plunges toward negative infinity, hugging that vertical line forever without ever reaching or crossing it.

faqs.question: Why does a logarithmic function never have a horizontal asymptote?
faqs.answer: A horizontal asymptote would mean the output levels off and approaches some fixed value as x grows without bound. But \( \log_b(x) \) keeps climbing forever, however slowly — it just never stops increasing. Since the output never settles near a fixed height, there's nothing for a horizontal asymptote to attach to.

faqs.question: What is the domain and range of the parent logarithmic function \( g(x) = \log_b(x) \)?
faqs.answer: The domain is (0, ∞) — only positive numbers are valid inputs, since that restriction is exactly what defines a logarithm (EL3). The range is all real numbers, (−∞, ∞) — the output can be any real number at all, since the graph climbs without any upper limit and plunges without any lower limit near the asymptote.

faqs.question: What are the x-intercept and y-intercept of the parent logarithmic function, and why is there no y-intercept?
faqs.answer: The x-intercept is always (1, 0), since any base raised to the power 0 equals 1, meaning \( \log_b(1) = 0 \) for every base. There is no y-intercept, because a y-intercept would require x = 0 to be a valid input — but 0 isn't in the domain (faq-4), so the graph can never touch the y-axis at all.

faqs.question: How does the graph of a logarithmic function relate to the graph of its inverse exponential function?
faqs.answer:
Since a logarithmic function is the inverse of its matching exponential function (EL3, FN6), their graphs are mirror images of each other across the line y = x. Every feature swaps accordingly: the exponential's horizontal asymptote becomes the logarithm's vertical asymptote, the exponential's y-intercept (0,1) becomes the logarithm's x-intercept (1,0), and the domain/range pair flips completely.

The two graphs are mirror images across y = x — the defining picture of any inverse function pair.

faqs.question: How does a horizontal shift affect the asymptote, domain, and range of a logarithmic function?
faqs.answer:
A horizontal shift moves the vertical asymptote by exactly the same amount as the shift, since the whole graph — including the vertical boundary it hugs — moves together sideways. The domain shifts along with the asymptote, but the range stays all real numbers either way.

Shifting left 1 moves the whole graph AND its asymptote left 1 — domain becomes (−1, ∞).

faqs.question: How does a vertical shift affect the asymptote, domain, and range of a logarithmic function?
faqs.answer: A vertical shift doesn't touch the asymptote, domain, or range at all — since the asymptote x = 0 is a vertical line, sliding the graph up or down doesn't change its horizontal position. The graph just slides vertically along that same unchanged boundary. Only the specific output values (and the x-intercept) change.

faqs.question: How does a reflection over the x-axis affect a logarithmic function's domain?
faqs.answer: It doesn't. A reflection over the x-axis \( (g(x) = -\log_b(x)) \) flips the graph upside down, but every x-value that was valid before is still exactly as valid afterward — flipping vertically never removes or adds any input values. The domain stays (0, ∞); only the shape of the curve inverts.

faqs.question: How does a reflection over the y-axis affect a logarithmic function's domain?
faqs.answer:
This one DOES change the domain. A reflection over the y-axis \( (h(x) = \log_b(-x)) \) flips the graph left-to-right, which flips which side of the asymptote is valid: instead of needing x > 0, you now need −x > 0, meaning x < 0. The domain flips from (0, ∞) to (−∞, 0).

Mirror images of each other across the y-axis — same asymptote, opposite side.

faqs.question: How do I find the domain, range, and asymptote of a transformed logarithmic function like \( j(x) = \log_4(x+1) \) or \( h(x) = \log_4(-x) \)?
faqs.answer:
The range is always (−∞, ∞) no matter what — transformations never change this for a logarithmic function. For the asymptote, start from x = 0 and apply only the horizontal shift and/or horizontal reflection (ignore vertical shifts and reflections — neither affects a vertical asymptote's position). The domain then follows directly from the asymptote and which side of it the graph occupies.
Worked Examples

\( j(x) = \log_4(x+1) \): horizontal shift left 1 → asymptote \( x=-1 \), domain \( (-1,\infty) \), range \( (-\infty,\infty) \)

\( h(x) = \log_4(-x) \): horizontal reflection only → asymptote \( x=0 \), domain \( (-\infty,0) \), range \( (-\infty,\infty) \)

faqs.question: How do I graph a transformed logarithmic function without plotting a full table of points?
faqs.answer: Start by sketching the parent curve's basic shape and its two anchor features: the vertical asymptote and the x-intercept (1, 0). Apply each transformation to those two anchors first — shift the asymptote line, shift or reflect the point — then redraw the same overall curve shape relative to the new anchors.

faqs.question: Why do the transformation rules for logarithmic functions seem "flipped" compared to exponential functions from EL2?
faqs.answer: Because logarithmic and exponential functions are inverses (faq-6), and inverses swap the roles of input and output. In EL2, vertical shifts (which act on the output) moved the asymptote and range, while horizontal shifts (which act on the input) left them alone. Here, since logarithms and exponentials have swapped domain/range roles, it's exactly reversed: horizontal shifts (acting on the now-restricted input) move the asymptote and domain, while vertical shifts leave them alone. Nothing is arbitrary here — it's the direct, predictable consequence of the inverse relationship.

faqs.question: Why do logarithmic graphs matter beyond this course?
faqs.answer: Logarithmic graphs describe a huge range of real phenomena that grow quickly at first and then level off in relative growth rate — learning curves, the relationship between an animal's size and its metabolism, or how perceived loudness relates to actual sound intensity. Understanding the shape, asymptote, and domain of a logarithmic graph also becomes essential for solving logarithmic and exponential equations later in this unit, since knowing where a function is even defined is the first step in solving any equation involving it.

paths.label: EL4: Graphs of Logarithmic Functions
paths.intro: Builds to the EL4 check: graphing logarithmic functions and finding their domain, range, and asymptote.

stages.desc: Two quick reviews EL4 leans on: evaluating logs (EL3) and inverses (FN6). Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Logs at 1, b, and 1/b
stops.target: Know the three easy log values: \(\log_b 1 = 0\), \(\log_b b = 1\), \(\log_b \tfrac{1}{b} = -1\). These become the key points of every log graph.
stops.coldPlain: Evaluate log_3 1, log_3 3, log_3 (1/3), and log_3 9.
stops.solution: Each log asks "3 to what power?" 3^0 = 1, 3^1 = 3, 3^(-1) = 1/3, 3^2 = 9.
stops.explain:
Why these values?

Every log is a question about an exponent: \(\log_b a\) asks "\(b\) to what power gives \(a\)?" Rewrite each one in exponential form and the answer comes from an exponent rule you already know.

Log questionRewrite as an exponentWhich power works?So the log is
\(\log_b 1 = \,?\)\(b^{?} = 1\)Any base to the 0 power is 1: \(b^0 = 1\)\(0\)
\(\log_b b = \,?\)\(b^{?} = b\)A number to the 1st power is itself: \(b^1 = b\)\(1\)
\(\log_b \tfrac{1}{b} = \,?\)\(b^{?} = \tfrac{1}{b}\)A negative exponent makes a reciprocal: \(b^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{b}\)\(-1\)
\(\log_b b^2 = \,?\)\(b^{?} = b^2\)The exponent is right there: 2\(2\)

That is why every log graph passes through \((1, 0)\) and \((b, 1)\): they come straight from \(b^0 = 1\) and \(b^1 = b\).

stops.title: Inverses swap x and y
stops.target: \(y = \log_b x\) is the inverse of \(y = b^x\), so its graph is the exponential graph with \(x\) and \(y\) swapped: a mirror image across \(y = x\).
stops.cold: The graph of \(y = 2^x\) passes through \((0, 1)\), \((1, 2)\), and \((2, 4)\), with horizontal asymptote \(y = 0\). What points and asymptote does \(y = \log_2 x\) have?
stops.coldPlain: The graph of y = 2^x passes through (0, 1), (1, 2), and (2, 4), with horizontal asymptote y = 0. What points and asymptote does y = log_2 x have?
stops.coldA: Swap each pair: \((1, 0)\), \((2, 1)\), \((4, 2)\). The horizontal asymptote \(y = 0\) becomes the vertical asymptote \(x = 0\).[[graph:SW]]
stops.solution: Inverse functions swap inputs and outputs, so swap each point: (0, 1) -> (1, 0), (1, 2) -> (2, 1), (2, 4) -> (4, 2). Swapping x and y also turns the horizontal line y = 0 into the vertical line x = 0.
stops.again: The range of \(y = 2^x\) is \((0, \infty)\) and its domain is \((-\infty, \infty)\). What are the domain and range of \(y = \log_2 x\)?
stops.reflect: Why does swapping \(x\) and \(y\) turn a horizontal asymptote into a vertical one?

stages.desc: The parent graph first, then each transformation the EL4 check uses, with what happens to the asymptote and domain.

stops.title: The parent graph
stops.target: Graph \(y = \log_b x\) from a table with \(x = \tfrac{1}{b}, 1, b, b^2\). Domain \((0, \infty)\), range \((-\infty, \infty)\), vertical asymptote \(x = 0\).
stops.cold: Make a table and graph \(y = \log_2 x\). State the domain, range, and asymptote.
stops.coldPlain: Make a table and graph y = log_2 x. State the domain, range, and asymptote.
stops.note: I graphed it on paper. I'll either upload a photo or describe it: the vertical asymptote, two labeled points, and which side of the asymptote the graph is on. Check my graph.
stops.coldA: Domain \((0, \infty)\), range \((-\infty, \infty)\), asymptote \(x = 0\). Choose \(x\)-values that are powers of 2 so the logs come out whole.[[graph:P2]]
stops.solution: Pick x-values that are powers of 2: 1/2, 1, 2, 4, 8 give y = -1, 0, 1, 2, 3. The graph climbs slowly to the right and dives down toward x = 0 without touching it.
stops.mistake: Picking x = 3 or 5 (the logs are not whole numbers), or letting the graph cross x = 0.
stops.again: Make a table and graph \(y = \log_3 x\).
stops.againA: Use \(x = \tfrac{1}{3}, 1, 3, 9\). Same domain, range, and asymptote.[[graph:P3]]
stops.reflect: Why do you pick \(x\)-values that are powers of the base?

stops.title: Shift up or down: the asymptote stays
stops.target: \(y = \log_b x + k\) moves every point up \(k\). A vertical shift does not move a vertical line, so the asymptote stays \(x = 0\) and the domain stays \((0, \infty)\).
stops.cold: Graph \(y = \log_2 x + 3\). State the domain, range, and asymptote.
stops.coldPlain: Graph y = log_2 x + 3. State the domain, range, and asymptote.
stops.note: I graphed it on paper. I'll either upload a photo or describe it: the vertical asymptote, two labeled points, and which side of the asymptote the graph is on. Check my graph.
stops.coldA: Add 3 to each \(y\). Domain \((0, \infty)\), range \((-\infty, \infty)\), asymptote \(x = 0\).[[graph:V1]]
stops.solution: Every y-value goes up 3: (1, 0) becomes (1, 3), (2, 1) becomes (2, 4). The asymptote is vertical, so shifting up does not move it.
stops.mistake: Moving the asymptote to x = 3 or y = 3.
stops.reflect: Compare with EL2: which kind of shift moved the exponential asymptote, and which moves the log asymptote?

stops.title: Shift left or right: the asymptote moves
stops.target: \(y = \log_b(x - h)\) shifts right \(h\) (left if \(x + h\)). The asymptote moves to \(x = h\) and the domain becomes \((h, \infty)\), where the argument is positive.
stops.cold: Graph \(y = \log_3(x - 2)\). State the domain and asymptote.
stops.coldPlain: Graph y = log_3(x - 2). State the domain and asymptote.
stops.note: I graphed it on paper. I'll either upload a photo or describe it: the vertical asymptote, two labeled points, and which side of the asymptote the graph is on. Check my graph.
stops.coldA: Asymptote \(x = 2\), domain \((2, \infty)\), range \((-\infty, \infty)\). The argument is 1 at \(x = 3\) (point \((3, 0)\)) and 3 at \(x = 5\) (point \((5, 1)\)).[[graph:H1]]
stops.solution: Set the argument to 0 for the asymptote: x - 2 = 0, x = 2. Domain from x - 2 > 0: (2, infinity). Points: x - 2 = 1 gives (3, 0); x - 2 = 3 gives (5, 1).
stops.mistake: Shifting left for x - 2, or plotting (1, 0) instead of (3, 0).
stops.reflect: How does "set the argument equal to 0" find the asymptote every time?

stops.title: Reflect across the x-axis
stops.target: \(y = -\log_b x\) flips every \(y\)-value, so the graph falls instead of rising. The asymptote and domain do not change.
stops.note: I graphed it on paper. I'll either upload a photo or describe it: the vertical asymptote, two labeled points, and which side of the asymptote the graph is on. Check my graph.
stops.coldA: Change the sign of each \(y\): \((1, 0)\), \((2, -1)\), \((4, -2)\). Asymptote \(x = 0\), domain \((0, \infty)\).[[graph:R1]]
stops.solution: Negating the output flips the graph over the x-axis. (1, 0) stays put; (2, 1) becomes (2, -1). The domain and the vertical asymptote are unchanged.
stops.mistake: Flipping the graph to the left side of the y-axis (that is a y-axis reflection).
stops.reflect: Which point stays put under this reflection, and why?

stops.title: Reflect across the y-axis
stops.target: \(y = \log_b(-x)\) flips the graph to the left of the \(y\)-axis. The domain becomes \((-\infty, 0)\), since \(-x\) must be positive.
stops.coldPlain: Graph y = log_2(-x). State the domain.
stops.note: I graphed it on paper. I'll either upload a photo or describe it: the vertical asymptote, two labeled points, and which side of the asymptote the graph is on. Check my graph.
stops.coldA: Domain \((-\infty, 0)\): \(-x > 0\) means \(x < 0\). Mirror each parent point: \((-1, 0)\), \((-2, 1)\), \((-4, 2)\).[[graph:Y1]]
stops.solution: The argument -x must be positive, so x < 0. Plug in x = -1: log_2(1) = 0. x = -2: log_2(2) = 1. x = -4: log_2(4) = 2. The graph is the parent mirrored across the y-axis; asymptote x = 0.
stops.mistake: Drawing it on the right side, or thinking log_2(-x) is always undefined (it is defined when x is negative).
stops.reflect: How can \(\log(-x)\) be defined? What must be true about \(x\)?

stages.desc: A practice check in the same three-part format as the EL4 CheckIt exercise.

stops.title: Practice check
stops.target: State the domain, range, and asymptote, and graph with two labeled points, the way the EL4 check asks.
stops.cold:
Let \(f(x) = -\log_4(x + 3)\).
(a) Find the domain and range in interval notation.
(b) Write the equation of any asymptotes.
(c) Graph \(f\). Label at least two points and draw any asymptotes with a dotted line.
stops.coldPlain: Let f(x) = -log_4(x + 3). (a) Domain and range in interval notation. (b) Equation of any asymptotes. (c) Graph f with two labeled points and dotted asymptotes.
stops.note: I graphed it on paper. I'll either upload a photo or describe it: the vertical asymptote, two labeled points, and which side of the asymptote the graph is on. Check my graph.
stops.solution: (a) x + 3 > 0 gives x > -3; every log has range all real numbers. (b) x + 3 = 0 gives x = -3. (c) x + 3 = 1 at x = -2 gives -log_4 1 = 0; x + 3 = 4 at x = 1 gives -log_4 4 = -1.
stops.mistake: Writing the range as (0, infinity) (that is the exponential range), or the asymptote as y = -3.
stops.again: Let \(f(x) = \log_6(-x) - 4\). Find (a) the domain and range, (b) the asymptote, and (c) graph with two labeled points.
stops.reflect: Which transformations move a log graph's asymptote, and which do not?
